Elena, Irene —

Following up with slightly more concrete technical guidance (see attached quantization-guidance.pdf and batching-latency-scenarios.png). Key points: 

1) Quantization recommendation
- Start with Q4 (4-bit) post-training quantization (PTQ) for Llama2-13B; expected quality delta: ~2% absolute on intent/classification metrics, ~3–6% on open-ended generation depending on prompt style. For any critical high-quality generation route, keep fp16 fallback.
- If you need tighter quality, run a small calibration set (we recommend ~10k in-domain samples) and evaluate QAT (quant-aware training) — usually 1–2 percentage points regain but costs/time increase.

2) Batching & latency tradeoffs
- If you adopt a 50ms aggregation window: depending on arrival rate you'll see a 20–40% reduction in per-request compute; median latency impact is near-zero for interactive users, but 95th percentile can increase by ~10–40ms depending on queueing.
- For strongly latency-sensitive endpoints (95th < 200ms), use adaptive single-request prioritization; for others, continuous batching is recommended.

3) KV cache impact
- With session affinity and cold-start warm-up, expect an 60–70% KV hit rate for chat sessions; that reduces token decode compute substantially for long sessions.

4) Economics (illustrative numbers)
- Example (per 1M tokens): fp16 baseline = $X; 4-bit quantized + batching/cache = ~35–50% lower compute cost in many workloads. The attached spreadsheet in the pilot MAP has sample rows.

Operational ask: to size discounts properly we need: expected monthly tokens, %of requests that are interactive chat, average context length, and acceptable 95th-latency SLO. If you can provide these, we will produce a final recommended commit band and the corresponding discount matrix.

-Mina
